verificationHistory.summary: (Major) Adoption story inconsistent across the doc graph: docs/platform-overview.md says integrated source under src/Libs/ is the only supported model and that NuGet packaging has not shipped yet, but src/Libs/Dabbler.Security/README.md still tells consumers to `dotnet add package Dabbler.Security` and src/Libs/Dabbler.Security.Blazor/README.md points readers at a NuGet-distributed core package.

(Major) The Round-1 fix to src/Libs/Dabbler.Security.Blazor/README.md was a partial fix: (a) Dependencies still contained a concrete https://www.nuget.org/packages/Dabbler.Security/ link pointing readers at a first-party NuGet-distributed package, and (b) the adoption note was over-broad — it said `NuGet packages (referenced in Dependencies below) ... have not shipped yet` which incorrectly swept in third-party packages like MudBlazor and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web that DO exist today. The Round-1 fix to src/Libs/Dabbler.Security/README.md was acceptable.

Verified: the concrete first-party NuGet link to Dabbler.Security has been replaced with a non-link bullet identifying integrated source today and a future NuGet release; the adoption note is now correctly scoped to first-party Dabbler packages and explicitly excludes third-party packages (MudBlazor, ASP.NET Core) from the 'not shipped yet' statement. No remaining inconsistency between src/Libs/Dabbler.Security.Blazor/README.md and docs/platform-overview.md.

scopeDeviations.rationale: Authoring-time decision per `feedback_avoid_upward_routing.md`. The gemini-pro draft was substantially shorter than the spec target (215 vs 300-500 lines) and missed shipped primitives in Components/Security sections. The orchestrator-side revision addressed every flagged gap directly (mechanical edit work using the source READMEs already in context). Net effect: routed cost stayed low ($0.0545 for the doc call) while the orchestrator absorbed the elaboration cost in conversation tokens. For canonical entry-point doc work, future sessions may want to seed the prompt with explicit per-section bullet lists or route to Sonnet (whose documentation template favors longer output) — calibration note recorded in ai-assignment.md actuals.

reason.specifics: Routed analysis (gemini-pro, $0.0019) recommended Claude Code Opus high for Session 4, aligning with the original spec ai-assignment recommendation of Opus moderate. Session 4 (Tri-Provider Platform Value Review) requires the orchestrator to (a) author its own architecture-level value assessment from scratch and (b) synthesize three independent provider reviews into a consolidated platform-value-review.md with gap dispositions. Both are exactly the 'Opus required for direct reasoning and synthesis' profile. The orchestrator-self-contributes-to-review-panel feedback memory applies: when the orchestrator's provider (Anthropic) is on the review panel, the orchestrator writes that perspective directly instead of routing Opus→Opus.

notes: Session 3 authored docs/platform-overview.md as the canonical entry-point doc for future platform consumers. The 3 verification rounds documented a useful pattern: cross-provider verification catching real consumer-facing inconsistencies the doc-refresh model alone missed. Round 1 surfaced the NuGet adoption-story mismatch (overview says integrated-source-only-today, but two per-library READMEs still said `dotnet add package Dabbler.Security`); Round 2 surfaced a sub-issue in the Round-1 fix (over-broad scope + lingering first-party NuGet link); Round 3 verified clean. Cost discipline note: the routed-cost-vs-orchestrator-cost balance for this session was again lopsided toward orchestrator-side reasoning (~$0.27 routed vs Opus medium conversation tokens). For canonical-doc-authoring sessions, an alternative routing pattern worth piloting in a future doc session is: route a section-by-section authoring pass (per-library section as separate route calls) rather than one big doc call, allowing the router's per-call complexity scoring to escalate naturally for the heaviest sections (Security, Components) while keeping the lighter sections (Reports.Export, Reports.Core) on cheaper models.
